evidence.claim: The IMF welcomed plans to phase out broad-based energy subsidies, support vulnerable groups, and prioritize productivity-enhancing spending in education, ICT, green-resilient infrastructure, and social protection, while also urging household-debt restructuring.
evidence.title: IMF Staff Completes 2022 Article IV Mission to Thailand
evidence.excerpt: The IMF welcomed plans to phase out broad-based energy subsidies, support vulnerable groups, and prioritize productivity-enhancing spending in education, ICT, green-resilient infrastructure, and social protection, while also urging household-debt restructuring.
evidence.source_locator: key paragraphs on targeted support, fiscal consolidation, and structural reform
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Same IMF mission statement, but this passage adds distinct policy guidance on spending quality and debt management.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 policy choices and the near-term policy mix.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirectly attributable to the Prayut government because it describes government policy options and implementation priorities, not a single personal order.
contrary_evidence: The IMF is advising the authorities, so the passage does not prove implementation success by itself.

evidence.claim: The FY2022 budget allocates 322,975.8 million baht to health and 453,891.2 million baht to education, and the education programme says it will reduce inequality, assist children with disabilities or special needs, and strengthen teachers and school quality.
evidence.title: THAILAND'S BUDGET IN BRIEF FISCAL YEAR 2022
evidence.publisher: Budget Bureau, Office of the Prime Minister
evidence.excerpt: The FY2022 budget allocates 322,975.8 million baht to health and 453,891.2 million baht to education, and the education programme says it will reduce inequality, assist children with disabilities or special needs, and strengthen teachers and school quality.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official budget tables and programme text set out the allocation and stated service goals.
evidence.period_fit: Direct FY2022 budget allocation and programme language.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government budget planning under Prayut's cabinet; the document does not isolate his personal role from the broader bureaucracy.
contrary_evidence: The allocation totals do not by themselves establish effective delivery or equal outcomes across regions and groups.

evidence.claim: The social opportunities and equality programme allocates 32,097.4 million baht to improve the lives of low-income people and farmers through the public welfare card, basic necessities, savings support, debt relief, and access to housing loans.
evidence.title: THAILAND'S BUDGET IN BRIEF FISCAL YEAR 2022
evidence.publisher: Budget Bureau, Office of the Prime Minister
evidence.excerpt: The social opportunities and equality programme allocates 32,097.4 million baht to improve the lives of low-income people and farmers through the public welfare card, basic necessities, savings support, debt relief, and access to housing loans.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: The budget brief explicitly names the programme and its target groups and instruments.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government policy under Prayut Chan-o-cha; the document does not show whether the benefits were politically neutral in practice.
contrary_evidence: The programme focus shows targeted support, but later World Bank and UNICEF reporting still found large rural poverty and child-wellbeing gaps.

evidence.claim: Thailand's cabinet approved 34.8 billion baht in cash subsidies for consumption, giving each person 1,200 baht to spend between February 1 and April 30 under an existing goods-purchase scheme.
evidence.title: Thailand approves $1 bln cash subsidy to boost consumption
evidence.excerpt: Thailand's cabinet approved 34.8 billion baht in cash subsidies for consumption, giving each person 1,200 baht to spend between February 1 and April 30 under an existing goods-purchase scheme.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a cabinet decision with specific amounts and dates.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Cabinet-level policy under Prayut Chan-o-cha, though the report does not separate his personal role from finance ministry implementation.
contrary_evidence: This was a temporary stimulus measure, so it shows crisis response more than durable social-development reform.

evidence.claim: After the House passed the first reading of the FY2023 budget bill, Prayut said the budget would support economic and social recovery after the crisis, help restore strong and sustained growth, reduce inequality, and distribute aid transparently across the country.
evidence.title: Parliament passes B3tn budget bill at first reading
evidence.excerpt: After the House passed the first reading of the FY2023 budget bill, Prayut said the budget would support economic and social recovery after the crisis, help restore strong and sustained growth, reduce inequality, and distribute aid transparently across the country.
evidence.source_locator: report body and attributed post-vote quote
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters-reported parliamentary coverage with a direct attributed quote from Prayut.
evidence.period_fit: June 2022 target-period budget debate and policy statement.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strongly attributable to Prayut as prime minister speaking in parliament, but it still reflects budget intent rather than delivery.
contrary_evidence: A first-reading budget statement is intent, not proof of implementation or distributive success.

evidence.claim: Thailand's economic stimulus policies would be more targeted toward vulnerable groups and low-income households, and fiscal policy would be more focused as the recovery continued.
evidence.title: Thai government spending to target low-income groups - Finance Minister
evidence.excerpt: Thailand's economic stimulus policies would be more targeted toward vulnerable groups and low-income households, and fiscal policy would be more focused as the recovery continued.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a finance-ministry statement about fiscal targeting.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government economic policy under Prayut's cabinet; the quote is from the finance minister rather than Prayut personally.
contrary_evidence: The statement is about future targeting, so it does not itself prove realised gains in 2022.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said Thailand's COVID fiscal response significantly mitigated the impact of the crisis on household welfare, but poverty was projected to rise as relief measures were phased out and more targeted social assistance was needed for elderly, disabled, and extreme-poor people.
evidence.title: Thailand’s Economy Remains Resilient amid Global Headwinds
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said Thailand's COVID fiscal response significantly mitigated the impact of the crisis on household welfare, but poverty was projected to rise as relief measures were phased out and more targeted social assistance was needed for elderly, disabled, and extreme-poor people.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: World Bank macro-fiscal monitor with explicit welfare and targeting judgments.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the target year and the late-2022 policy environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to Prayut's government because it concerns fiscal response and social-assistance choices, but it also reflects broader macro conditions and prior relief design.
contrary_evidence: The same source warns that welfare gains were incomplete and that poverty could rise again as emergency support ended.

evidence.claim: The ministry launched a mobile application for the child subsidy programme to reduce travel costs, prevent data-entry errors, and let families check entitlement status immediately, improving access to the child grant.
evidence.title: Mobile Application เงินเด็ก launches to improve access to the newborn child subsidy
evidence.publisher: Department of Older Persons, Ministry of Social Development and Human Security
evidence.excerpt: The ministry launched a mobile application for the child subsidy programme to reduce travel costs, prevent data-entry errors, and let families check entitlement status immediately, improving access to the child grant.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official ministry event notice with a concrete service-delivery change, though the web snapshot is brief and mirror-like.
evidence.period_fit: Direct target-year administrative action in September 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the Prayut government and social-development bureaucracy, but the page does not show cabinet-level design or measured impact.
contrary_evidence: The notice shows an access improvement, but it does not prove nationwide uptake or that the grant reached all eligible families.

unresolved_gaps: No direct 2022 ruler-attributed existential-risk choice, escalation, or crisis-management episode is shown.
Command-and-control, custody, and safety-governance evidence tied specifically to Prayut remains thin.
PM-level attribution for 2022 international-security choices is still thin; most evidence is ministry or delegation posture.
The Myanmar and Ukraine material does not yet show concrete peace or accountability outcomes attributable to Prayut.
Direct chain-of-command evidence for the APEC crackdown and the deep-south emergency regime remains limited.
The torture/disappearance law is an important reform, but year-end enforcement evidence is still weak.
Direct evidence on the sponsors and mechanism of the election-system change is still thin.
4B.4 and 4B.7 remain under-evidenced relative to the stronger protest, media, and term-limit material.
Budget intent and macro recovery are better evidenced than actual implementation and take-up.
Evidence on appointments, anti-capture, and mistake-correction is still weak.
Direct service-delivery, take-up, and quality evidence is thin outside budget allocations and national surveys.
Ruler-specific causal attribution for rural, child, and mental-health outcomes remains weak.
No independent 2022 finding of personal lying, self-dealing, or concealed conflict of interest is shown.
The package relies too much on allegations, self-defense, and broader regime context.
The program basis is only partly explicit; some objectives are inferred from budgets and coalition moves rather than a single frozen program statement.
Outcome evidence is sectoral and mixed, and external reopening effects remain hard to separate from ruler skill.
